name: Aung San Suu Kyi
role: Burmese politician; leader of the National League for Democracy; State Counsellor and foreign minister of Myanmar (2016-2021)
summary: Aung San Suu Kyi led the nonviolent movement for multi-party democracy and the rule of law in Burma, grounded in human rights, fearlessness and a revolution of the spirit. As State Counsellor she led a government that pursued constitutional change against the military's veto while prosecuting critics, defending the army over the Rohingya crisis and leaving the 1982 Citizenship Law in place.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The economic policy her government released aimed at a market-oriented economy and encouraged foreign investment, with small and medium enterprises as job creators.

public-ownership.rationale: The economic policy her government released envisaged possible privatisation of adaptable and lucrative state-owned businesses, and her planning minister spoke of reducing state ownership.

property-fundamental.rationale: The economic policy her government released promised to protect people's property and intellectual-property rights.

nation-first.rationale: She said that as members of one nation Myanmar's people also belong to the world, stressed the role of the United Nations, and said sharing values and wealth will create a better world for all.

revolution-justified.rationale: She welcomed the Tunisian and Egyptian revolutions and said those who take up arms to free themselves from unjust domination are freedom fighters whom she never condemned, though she chose non-violence for Burma.

one-party-rule.rationale: She demanded that the one-party system be dismantled and a multi-party system established through free and fair elections.

democracy-best.rationale: She called democracy the only ideology consistent with freedom, quoting her father, and said she fights for democracy because democratic institutions are necessary to guarantee human rights.

political-violence-never.rationale: She said she does not hold to non-violence on moral grounds but on practical political grounds, never condemned those who took up arms, and said she would support violence if a short burst would prevent worse things.

war-builds-character.rationale: She described the First World War as a terrifying waste of youth and potential and said suffering and war degrade and embitter.

ethnic-nation.rationale: She said Burma is a country of many ethnic nationalities whose future rests on a true spirit of union, and that the majority people should show restraint and tolerance towards the others.

universal-morality.rationale: She said democracy and human rights are the birthright of all, citing the Universal Declaration's rights for all human beings regardless of race, nationality or religion.

class-collaboration.rationale: She said she wants investors to profit and that the fruit of investment should be shared between the people and the investors.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: She said that in Burma women have no participation in the higher levels of government and none in the judiciary, and called for mutual respect instead of patriarchal domination and degradation.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Her government refused meaningful cooperation with UN investigators and left military impunity in place, according to Human Rights Watch.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Her government left the 1982 Citizenship Law, which stripped Rohingya of citizenship rights, unamended, and Rohingya remained confined and unable to return on equal terms, according to Human Rights Watch.

consent-of-governed.rationale: She criticised governments whose authority is founded on coercion rather than on the mandate of the people.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: She said Myanmar intends good relations with all its neighbours on a non-aligned pattern that has served it since independence.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: She said Myanmar advocates a world free of nuclear weapons and announced its ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

refugee-return.rationale: Her government's repatriation attempts required Rohingya to enter a verification process identifying them as foreigners, with no guarantee of citizenship and transit centres built on razed villages, according to Human Rights Watch.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The NLD she leads proposed amendments cutting the military's fixed seats in parliament and its veto, which the military blocked, according to Human Rights Watch.

religious-nation.rationale: She said Myanmar should not be a nation divided by religious beliefs, ethnicity or political ideology, and that everyone has the right to their diverse identity within one nation.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Asked whether she would keep Myanmar non-aligned, she said yes, and that it should not be a battleground between the United States and China.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: She wrote that just laws help preserve human dignity, and said human rights should be protected by the rule of law.

open-government-data.rationale: She said people should know what laws and decisions are under way before they are taken so that they can protest, support or make suggestions.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: She said the relationship between men and women should be characterised by partnership, trust and mutual respect, not patronising behaviour, exploitation or patriarchal domination.

women-distinct-values.rationale: She credited women with their capacity for compassion and self-sacrifice and said the education and empowerment of women will bring a more caring, tolerant, just and peaceful life.

open-diplomacy.rationale: She said bilateral projects, investments and aid agreements must be transparent, since the people of Burma were kept in the dark about contracts, which endangers national reconciliation.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Her government ordered an internet blackout in eight Rakhine townships and Paletwa from June 2019 that was still partly in force at year end, according to Human Rights Watch.

women-suffrage.rationale: She said people must be allowed a significant role in the governance of their country and that people include women, who make up at least half of the world's population.

no-business-privileges.rationale: She said she does not want investment to mean greater privileges for the already privileged, worried about investment that empowers the wrong circles and asked tourists to avoid crony-owned facilities.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: She called the use of religious propaganda against her party in the 2015 campaign wrong and unconstitutional, since the constitution says religion must not be used for political purposes.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: She wrote that each person must make sacrifices to win freedom and that victims of oppression must draw on their own resources to defend their rights, and said that dissidents come to terms early with the possibility of giving their lives.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: She called the constitution's state ownership of all land a big problem, since farmers cannot use land as collateral, and said it needs to be sorted out.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: She said she has never condemned and never will condemn students who formed armed forces after the 1988 killings, since those who take up arms to free themselves from unjust domination are freedom fighters.

notes: First audit. Sources read in full: Freedom from Fear (as posted in the Online Burma Library archive), the 1988 Shwedagon speech, the 2012 Nobel lecture, her 2016 UN General Assembly statement, the 2017 Rakhine speech and her ICJ statement of 2019; her record as State Counsellor is cited from Human Rights Watch reports of it (prosecutions of critics, the failed constitutional amendments, the 1982 Citizenship Law, the Rakhine internet blackout, repatriation terms) and answers alone where it exists. Also read: the BBC Reith Lectures 2011 (lectures 1 and 2 with questions), her 2015 Washington Post interview as reprinted, the 2012 World Economic Forum press conference captions, her 2017 Panglong opening speech (federal union aims, no statement that settles the bank's regional-autonomy statements), and press reports of her government's 12-point economic policy (2016). Also read (MediaSum, speaker-labelled CNN and NPR transcripts, searched by theme): CNN Amanpour 2012 and 2015 interviews, NPR 2012, CNN Zakaria 2016; they add her positions on investment and privilege and confirm the practical, not moral, case for non-violence. Also read: her 1995 keynote to the NGO Forum on Women and the 2012 Slate interview (Lally Weymouth). YouTube refused captions after the first requests, so the BBC and CNN interviews could not be read; the BBC 2013 and 2017 interviews exist only as press quotations (her 2017 remark that ethnic cleansing is too strong an expression is quoted in an NPR transcript, a report of words rather than a transcript of the interview). Themes searched: government and elections, rule of law, liberty, the army, violence and revolution, ethnic peace and federalism, refugees and citizenship, war and nuclear arms, economy, gender, religion and nationalism. Her own texts say little on economy, class, secularism, gender, monarchy and nationalism, and the interview transcripts that might (Irrawaddy, Washington Post, BBC) were refused or not found in full, so most statements are null and the uncertainty rule fails; that is the honest result.
